0. Overview of the lecture¶

  • In many applications, linear models do not capture the reality (according to Box's quote, they are not useful) and we have to consider non-linear models

  • There are two types of nonlinear regression models

    • parametric non-linear regression: the form of the regression equation is a nonlinear, but prespecified, function that is parametrized by finite number of parameters

    • non-parametric regression: the form of the regression equation is not prespecified. Instead, one finds the best function in a general function space (say set of continuous functions or smooth functions, etc.) that best "fits" the data according to some criterion

  • In this lecture, we see how to fit a parametric non-linear regression (non-parametric regression will be discussed in the next lecture).

  • We then discuss three classes of common parametric non-linear regression models

    • TBS and Cox-Box transformation: used for remedying abnormalities such as non-constant variance and non-normality

    • logit (or logistic) regression: used for classification task (predicting types instead of values)

    • Robust regression: regression models that are less sensitive to outliers

1. Parametric non-linear regression¶

  • The general parametric regression model:
\begin{align*} Y_n = f(\Xv_n;\betav) + \eps_n;\quad n\in\{1,\dots,N\} \end{align*}
  • $\{(Y_n, \Xv_n)\}_{n=1}^N$ is a sample of observations
  • $f$ is a known function (called the regression equation or function)
  • $\betav=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p)$ is a vector of unknown parameters
  • $\{\eps_n\}_{n=1}^N$ are white noise (that is, they are i.i.d. with zero mean and finite variance)
  • $\betav$ is estimated by non-linear least squares (NLS) estimator:
\begin{align*} \betavh = \underset{\betav}{\arg\min}\,\sum_{n=1}^N \Big(Y_n - f(\Xv_n;\betav)\Big)^2. \end{align*}
  • Many statistical softwares (including R) have functions that numerically obtain NLS estimators
  • Once $\betav$ is found, the fitted values are $\Yh_n = f(\Xv_n;\betavh)$ and the residuals are $\epsh_n=Y_n-\Yh_n$
  • Diagnostic of parametric regression models is similar to diagnostic of linear regression model

  • One should check that:

    • There is no systematic pattern in the residuals: plot raw residuals vs. fitted values

    • Residuals are uncorrelated (e.g. ACF plot of the residuals)

    • Residuals have constant conditional variance: use the plot of raw absolute residual vs. fitted values

  • It is possible to define externally studentized residuals (rstudent) for nonlinear models. However, in this course, it suffices to use the raw residuals for diagnostics of parametric non-linear models
  • As an example, consider the relationship between credit rating of a company $X$ and its probability of default $Y$
  • We look at a sample of companies over a period. The credit ratings are labeled as 1 (the best credit rating of AAA) to 16 (the worst credit rating of B3)
  • Let $Y_n$ be the percentage of the companies with credit rating $X_n$ that defaulted over a fixed period of time

  • We propose the following parametric regression models \begin{align*} Y_n = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n + \eps_n};\quad \eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1) \end{align*} and \begin{align*} Y_n = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n} + \eps_n;\quad \eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1) \end{align*}
  • Q: Do you see the difference between these two models?
  • The first model is a linear multiple regression model "in disguise"
  • We can re-write it as follows: define $\tilde{Y}_n=\log Y_n$, such that
\begin{align*} \tilde{Y}_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n + \eps_n;\quad \eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1) \end{align*}
  • We can use OLS (ordinary least squares) to fit this model
  • The second model is truly non-linear. It can be fitted by NLS
  • Some nonlinearities are "removable"

  • For example, polynomial regression mode, $f(x;\betav) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,x + \dots + \beta_p\,x^p$

    can be transform to a linear multiple regression model. Can you guess how?

  • Read section 11.7 of the textbook for further information
  • Let us fit the first model, that is
\begin{align*} \log Y_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n + \eps_n;\quad \eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1) \end{align*}
  • To fit the first model, we need to drop the 0 frequencies (why?)

  • Since we don't transform the response, there is no need to drop the zero frequencies observations!
  • To fit the second model, we can use the R function nls().
  • It uses an iterative optimization method, so, we need to give it an initial guess for the parameters using the argument start=

  • The residuals seem to have non-constant variance. They are also not normal due to heavy tails.
  • In the next section, we use a transformation to remedy these abnormalities

2. Transforming response and/or predictors¶

  • Most often, we can improve a model by applying it to the transformed data.
  • We have already seen one example. In the corporate v.s. government example, we mentioned that it is better to find a model between the rate changes rather than rates. In that example, we transformed the data by differencing.
  • Next, we discuss two types of transformations that can be used for correcting abnormalities in Regression models.

2.1 Transform-both-sides (TBS) regression¶

  • The TBS regression is mainly used as a remedy for non-constant variance or non-normality of residuals
  • Consider a model without noise $Y_n = f(\Xv_n;\betav)$
  • For any monotonic function $h$ (that is, an increasing or a decreasing function), this model is equivalent to $h(Y_n) = h\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)$
  • In a TBS regression, one applies a monotonic function to both the response variable and the regression function

  • In other words, the original model \begin{align*} \\ \qquad\qquad\qquad Y_n = f(\Xv_n;\betav) + \eps_n;\quad n\in\{1,\dots,N\} \end{align*}

    is replaced by

\begin{align*} h(Y_n) = h\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right) + \epst_n;\quad n\in\{1,\dots,N\} \end{align*}
  • Note, however, that the two models are not equivalent because of the noise term
  • TBS regression is a parametric nonlinear regression model and can be estimated by NLS
  • Let us consider the default rate example $Y_n = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n} + \eps_n;~\eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1)$
  • The residual diagnostic revealed that the residuals are not normal and do not have constant variance
In [10]:
par(mfrow=c(1,2));par(mar=c(4,4,4,4))
plot(fitted(fit_NLS),abs(resid(fit_NLS)),
     xlab="fitted values", ylab="absolute residual")
fit_loess  = loess(abs(resid(fit_NLS))~ fitted(fit_NLS),span=1,deg=1)
ord_NLS = order(fitted(fit_NLS))
lines(fitted(fit_NLS)[ord_NLS],fit_loess$fit[ord_NLS], col="red")
qqnorm(resid(fit_NLS),datax=T,main="",ylab="sample quantiles",
       xlab="theoretical quantiles")
qqline(resid(fit_NLS),datax=T, col="red")
  • To remedy these issues, we consider the TBS regression obtained by taking the square root of both sides
\begin{align*} \sqrt{Y_n} = e^{0.5\,\beta_0 + 0.5\, \beta_1 X_n} + \epst_n;~~~~~~~~~\eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1) \end{align*}

  • How does TBS works? How do we find the "correct" transformation function?
  • TBS regression works by assigning weights to observations in the sum of squares errors
  • To see this, consider Taylor's expansion of the NLS objective function for a TBS regression
\begin{align*} \sum_{n=1}^N \left[h(Y_n) - h\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)\right]^2 &\approx \sum_{n=1}^N \left[h'\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)\left(Y_n-f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)\right]^2\\ &= \sum_{n=1}^N \left[h'\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)\right]^2\left[Y_n-f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right]^2 \end{align*}
  • The NLS objective function for the original model is $\sum_{n=1}^N \left[Y_n-f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right]^2$
  • Therefore, TBS regression effectively assigns weights to observations, the weight for the n-th observation is $\left[h'\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)\right]^2$
  • One of the main use of TBS regression is to restore constant variance of residuals
  • To this end, the weights in TBS should be inversely proportional to the conditional variance of response given predictors
\begin{align}\tag{$\star$} \left[h'\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)\right]^2\propto \frac{1}{\Var(Y_n|\Xv_n)} \end{align}
  • This relationship can be used to identify an appropriate $h$ in the TBS regression
  • Let us see how to find the "variance stabilizing transformation" in the default rate example
  • The default rate $Y_n$ in the previous example can be seen as the number of defaults (per each credit score category) divided by a fixed number (i.e. the total number of companies in that category)
  • Can you suggest a distribution for $Y_n|\Xv_n$?
  • We can choose Poisson or binomial distribution. Calculations are simpler with Poisson.
  • We assume that $Y_n|\Xv_n$ is Poisson with conditional mean (and variance) of $f(\Xv_n;\betav)$
  • To find a function h that stabilizes the variance of errors, we may use equation $(\star)$
\begin{align*} \left[h'\left(f(\Xv_n;\betav)\right)\right]^2\propto \frac{1}{\Var(Y_n|\Xv_n)} = \frac{1}{f(\Xv_n;\betav)} \end{align*}
  • Therefore, $h$ must satisfy $h'(x) = \frac{k}{\sqrt{x}}$, for some constant $k\ne0$
  • By integrating both sides, we obtain $h(x) = 2\,k \sqrt{x} + C$, where $k$ and $C$ are arbitrary constants and $(\star)$ holds for any choice of their values
  • For example, we may choose $k=1/2$ and $C=0$ to obtain $h(x)=\sqrt{x}$
  • This yields the TBS regression that we fitted above
  • Note that to find the variance stabilizing TBS regression, we had to make assumption on the distribution of the response, that is, we assumed it is Poisson
  • In general, to find the variance stabilizing TBS regression, we needed to make distributional assumptions
  • The next transformation takes a more "agnostic" approach.

2.2. Box-Cox transformation¶

  • This transformation is also used for correcting abnormalities in regression diagnostic, such as non-normality or non-constant variance of residuals
  • Only the response variable is transformed
\begin{align*} Y_n^\al = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, X_{n,1} + \dots + \beta_p\,X_{n,p} + \eps_n;\quad n\in\{1,\dots,N\} \end{align*}
  • Here, $\al$, $\beta_0$, ..., $\beta_p$ are unknown parameters to be estimated
  • The parameters are estimated by the profile MLE method, which we explain next (profile MLE is discussed in section 5.15 of the textbook)
  • Let $L(\al, \betav)$ be the likelihood function in MLE for the parameters. Then,
\begin{align*} L(\alh_\text{ML},\betavh_\text{ML}) = \underset{\al,\betav}{\max} L(\al, \betav) = \underset{\al}{\max}\Big\{\underset{\betav}{\max} L(\al, \betav)\Big\} \end{align*}
  • Let us define
\begin{align*} L_{\max}(\al)=\underset{\betav}{\max} L(\al, \betav) \end{align*}
  • We then have
\begin{align*} \alh_\text{ML} := \underset{\al}{\arg\max}\,L_{\max}(\al), \end{align*}
  • This motivates the following two-step approach
  • Step 1: Draw the function $L_\max(\al)$ and choose its maximizer. Usually, a "round value" near the maximizer of $L_\max(\al)$ is chosen. Let us denote it by $\alh$
  • Step2: We obtain the estimator $\betavh$ by fitting the following multiple linear regression model (using OLS):
\begin{align*} Y_n^{\alh} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, X_{n,1} + \dots + \beta_p\,X_{n,p} + \eps_n;\quad n\in\{1,\dots,N\} \end{align*}
  • Note that Box-Cox transformation is designed for multiple linear regression, so, we cannot apply it to remedy the non-constant variance of model 2 in the default example
  • Let us illustrate Box-Cox transformation by a new example using simulated data
In [14]:
n = 80
set.seed("781235")
e = matrix(runif(12*n),nrow=n) %*% rep(1,12)
e = abs(e)^4
e= e/mean(e) 
x1 = runif(n)
x1 = sort(x1) 
x2 = rbeta(n,6,.5)
y = (8*x2 + x1 + 5*x1^3) + ( 4* x2 + x1 + 7*x1^3) * e
pairs(~y+x1+x2)
  • We consider fitting a polynomial regression
\begin{align*} Y_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{n,1} + \beta_2 X_{n,1}^2 + \beta_3 X_{n,2} + \eps_n \end{align*}

  • Next, we correct the abnormalities by Box-Cox transformation
  • To obtain $\alh$ in the first step of profile MLE, we can use boxcox() function in MASS package
  • The default domain is $[-2,2]$. If the maximum is not attained, use the argument lambda = seq(a, b, 1/10) to change the domain to $[a,b]$
In [17]:
library(MASS)
L_max = boxcox(y ~ x1 + I(x1^2) + x2,ylab="log-likelihood")
  • We can obtain the exact value of the maximizer of $L_\max(\al)$ as follows. It is acceptable to use the nearest round value, say $-1$
In [18]:
alphahat = L_max$x[which.max(L_max$y)]
alphahat
-0.828282828282828
  • Next, we find the estimates for $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, and $\beta_3$ by fitting the transformed model $Y_n^\alh = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{n,1} + \beta_2 X_{n,1}^2 + \beta_3 X_{n,2} + \eps_n$
In [19]:
y2 = y^alphahat
fit_BoxCox = lm(y2 ~ x1 + I(x1^2) + x2)
summary(fit_BoxCox)

3. Logit regression¶

  • Classification can be seen as a regression problem where the response variable is discrete and takes finite number of values, say $\{0, 1, 2,\dots,K-1\}$
  • Example: spam filter; classifying news as good, bad, or neutral; classifying faces as male or female
  • In machine learning literature, regression and classification are seen as two different tasks. Regression is about predicting values while the goal of classification is to predict categories
  • Here, we only consider binary classification, where there are only two categories (i.e. $K=2$), which we label as 0 and 1
  • We discuss a parametric regression model for the binary classification problem
  • Classification problems are more thoroughly discussed in CFRM 521
  • Consider the regression model $Y_n = f(\Xv_n;\betav)+\eps_n$, where $Y_n\in\{0,1\}$
  • Can we fit this model using NLS (or OLS if $f(\Xv_n;\betav)$ is linear in $\betav$)?
  • The answer is negative.
  • We have
\begin{align*} f(\Xv_n;\betav) = \Eb(Y_n|\Xv_n) = \Pb(Y_n=1|\Xv_n) \end{align*}
  • Therefore
\begin{align*} 0\le f(\Xv_n;\betav)\le1 \end{align*}
  • We need to take this constraint into account
  • This can be done using generalized linear models (GLM), which we discuss next
  • In GLM, we consider the parametric non-linear model
\begin{align*} Y_n = H(\beta_0 + \beta_1\,X_{n,1} + \dots + \beta_p\,X_{n,p}) + \eps_n \end{align*}
  • For binary classification, $H(x)$ is a CDF function (i.e. a non-decreasing function that satisfies $\lim_{x\to-\infty}H(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty}H(x)=1$)

  • Two common choices of $H$ are:

    • Probit regression: H is the standard normal CDF given by $\displaystyle H(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x\frac{\ee^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\dd x$

    • Logit regression: H is the logistic CDF given by $\displaystyle H(x) = \frac{1}{1+\ee^{-x}}$

  • Once $H(x)$ is chosen, the parameters $\beta_0$,..., $\beta_p$ are estimated by Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
  • Note that for the binary response model, $Y_n|\Xv_n$ are i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p=\Pb(Y_n=1|\Xv_n) = f(\Xv_n;\betav)$ (as we have shown before)
  • Let us calculate the likelihood function of a sample $Y_1,\dots,Y_N$, if the true values of the regression parameters are $\betav$
\begin{align*} L(\betav) &=\prod_{n=1}^N \Big[\Pb(Y_n=1|\Xv_n)\Big]^{Y_n}\Big[\Pb(Y_n=0|\Xv_n)\Big]^{1-Y_n}\\ &=\prod_{n=1}^N \Big[H(\beta_0 + \beta_1\,X_{n,1} + \dots + \beta_p\,X_{n,p})\Big]^{Y_n}\\ &\qquad\qquad\Big[1-H(\beta_0 + \beta_1\,X_{n,1} + \dots + \beta_p\,X_{n,p})\Big]^{1-Y_n} \end{align*}
  • The maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of the model parameter is
\begin{align*} \betavh_\text{ML} = \underset{\betav}{\arg\max}\, L(\betav) \end{align*}
  • To solve this optimization problem, we need to use a numerical method
  • Let us fit a binary classification model using R
  • We use the dataset CreditCard in the R package AER, which contains various information about applicants for a certain credit card, along with the outcome of the application (stored in the column card)
  • See Example 11.7 in Section 11.6 of the textbook for a description of the data
  • The following code load the data and remove nonsensical observations (the ones with applicant age less than 18)

  • Based on this data, we would like to come up with a model to accept or reject applications
  • We take card as the response variable and the application information as the predictors
  • This problem can be solved by a binary response regression (since the response variable, card, takes only two values yes or no)
  • As can be seen from the histogram of the predictor, some are very skewed, which result in high-leverage points. To correct this, we replace the skewed variables with their logarithm

4. Robust regression¶

  • A robust estimator is designed not to be affected by outliers
  • There are many robust regression methods. Here, we consider the least-trimmed sum of squares (LTS) estimator
  • Consider a regression model $Y_n = f(\Xv_n;\betav) + \eps_n$

  • Define the trimmed sum of squares (TSS) as follows. For each value of $\betav$:

    • Let $\eps_n(\betav) = Y_n - f(\Xv_n;\betav)$, for $n\in\{1,\dots, N\}$

    • Order $\eps_n(\betav)^2$, remove 5% of the observations with largest values of $\eps_n(\betav)^2$. Let $I_0(\betav)$ denote the indices of the remaining 95% of the observations

    • Define the TSS$\displaystyle(\betav):= \sum_{n\in I_0(\betav)}\Big(Y_n-f(\Xv_n;\betav)\Big)^2$

  • To estimate the parameters, we minimize TSS$(\beta)$
  • Next, we illustrate LTS regression using the example we used for regression diagnostic
In [30]:
# simulating samples
set.seed(99)
x = 1:11
x[11] = 50
y=1+x+rnorm(11)
y2 = y
y2[11] = y[11]-45
x2 = x
x2[11] = 5.5
cexx = c(rep(21,10),19)
start = c(1,1,1,1)
  • The ltsReg() function in robustbase package can be used for LTS regression
In [31]:
library("robustbase")
summary(ltsReg(y2~x))
